draft.title: Building character through narration
card: Focalisation
Focalisation is whose eyes and mind a story is seen through. A reader learns about a character from what the focaliser notices, assumes and leaves out.
Reported speech
A character's words can be given in direct speech, in quotation marks, or in indirect speech, where the narrator sums them up. Indirect speech can make a character seem less heard or less reliable.
Example
Tom is seen through his sister's eyes: "Tom claimed he was just helping, as usual." The words "claimed" and "as usual" show her doubt, so the reader sees Tom as she does.
Effect
These choices shape character indirectly. The reader is guided to trust, pity or doubt a character without being told outright.
draft.remember: How a story is focalised and how words are reported can shape a character as much as description.

a.q: Why might a writer tell a story through one character's eyes?
opts: It shapes how the reader judges every character
It lets the narrator avoid describing anyone
It makes every character speak in direct speech
It shows the events from every character's view
a.why: Focalisation filters what the reader sees, so it guides how characters are judged. It does not give every view, because one mind controls what is noticed.
a.clue: Think about what one person notices and leaves out.

b.q: In Mia's story, Ravi is seen through his teacher: "Ravi muttered some excuse about homework, as he always did." What does this narration suggest about Ravi?
opts: The teacher doubts him, so the reader may doubt him too
Ravi is honest, because his words are quoted exactly
Ravi is shy, because the narrator says he muttered
The narrator is neutral, as no opinion is given
b.why: The words "some excuse" and "as he always did" show the teacher's doubt, and the reader sees Ravi through it. The wrong option about shyness is tempting, but the phrasing points to doubt, and the words are summed up, not quoted.
b.clue: Look at which words show the teacher's opinion.
